# Results — Study 168 (Advance-Decline) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Advance-Decline line is built
from daily returns of S&P 500 constituents (current membership — survivorship-biased panel,
see caveat below). SPY daily OHLCV from Yahoo Finance. A bearish divergence is flagged when
SPY is at a **63-day high** while the cumulative A/D line is NOT at its 63-day high, and SPY
has risen at least 3% over the window. Forward returns are the 21-day log-return for SPY
starting the day after the signal. As-of **2026-06-15**.*

---

## Data stamp

| Series | Window | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|
| SPY daily (Yahoo, auto-adjusted) | 2005-01-03 -> 2026-06-12 | `8e7f69ef9d75` |
| S&P 500 constituent panel (497 tickers) | 2005-01-04 -> 2026-06-12 | — |

**Survivorship bias acknowledged:** the constituent panel is current S&P 500 membership
projected backwards. Delisted names (losers) are absent. For breadth measurement this means
firms that declined enough to be removed from the index are excluded from our A/D counts —
the bias likely overstates breadth and could either inflate or deflate the divergence signal
frequency. This is named on the Signal axis. A control that shares the bias (all days vs
divergence days, within the same biased panel) can support existence but not magnitude.

---

## Primary test: 63-day lookback, 21-day forward horizon

*n = 307 bearish divergence signals over ~21 years (avg ~14.6/yr). Benchmark: 4,784 valid
forward-return observations (all non-NaN days with full 21-day window).*

| Arm | n | mean fwd-return | HAC t | hit-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Post-divergence (bearish signal)** | 307 | **+95.8 bps** | **+3.35** | 71.3% |
| Unconditional baseline (all days) | 4,784 | **+87.3 bps** | **+4.73** | 67.3% |

**Difference (divergence minus baseline): +8.5 bps** (divergence days are SLIGHTLY
BETTER, not worse, than the unconditional baseline).

> The bearish divergence signal does not predict below-average forward returns — in the
> primary specification, divergence periods are fractionally *above* the baseline. This
> is the opposite of the claim.

Permutation p-value (fraction of 2,000 random sub-samples of size 307 more negative
than the observed divergence mean): **0.608** — the divergence sub-sample is not unusual
in the tails of the random-sub-sample distribution.

---

## Lookback sweep (21-day forward horizon)

*How does the signal behave across different lookback windows?*

| Lookback (days) | n signals | post-div mean (bps) | base mean (bps) | diff (bps) | div HAC t |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 21 | 221 | +104.8 | +87.3 | **+17.5** | +3.18 |
| 42 | 288 | +111.4 | +87.3 | **+24.1** | +3.79 |
| 63 | 307 | +95.8 | +87.3 | **+8.5** | +3.35 |
| 126 | 284 | +72.5 | +87.3 | **−14.8** | +2.45 |
| 252 | 273 | +72.1 | +87.3 | **−15.2** | +2.37 |

The sign of the divergence-vs-baseline difference flips across lookbacks (positive for
short windows, negative for longer windows). This is a hallmark of specification search:
there is no stable direction. The "bearish divergence" recipe would require cherry-picking
a lookback window and horizon to get even a weak bearish result.

---

## Drawdown analysis (63-day post-signal window)

| Window | Mean max drawdown | N events |
|---|--:|--:|
| Post-divergence signal (63d) | **−6.3%** | 307 |
| Unconditional (all 63d windows, sampled) | **−7.2%** | ~945 |

Post-divergence max drawdown is actually *smaller* (less severe) than the unconditional
baseline — again the opposite of the bearish claim.

---

## Tradability

Even if the signal were bearish, the recipe implies shorting SPY (or buying put options)
for ~1 month at each divergence:

| Round-trip cost assumption | Post-div gross (21d) | Net |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +95.8 bps | +95.8 bps (but the trade is SHORT SPY!) |
| 10 bps ETF round-trip | +95.8 bps | +85.8 bps |

Because the signal is *bullish* (not bearish) in the real data, a short position would
lose ~86–96 bps/trade on average. The expected direction of the trade is wrong.

---

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The bearish A/D divergence signal does NOT predict below-baseline
  forward returns. Across all tested lookbacks and horizons, the divergence arm is
  indistinguishable from or *above* the unconditional baseline. The claim — *"generals
  advancing, soldiers retreating signals a top"* — is unsupported on this tape.
- **Survivorship bias named on Signal axis.** The constituent panel is biased toward
  survivors; a true point-in-time panel could shift the result but the direction of
  the shift is not obvious for breadth measurement.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even setting aside that the signal points the wrong way,
  ~14.6 signals/year (one per ~17 trading days) with unreliable forward direction
  and meaningful transaction costs makes this uneconomic.
- **Third axis — Coincident, not leading.** The A/D line is largely coincident with
  the index (high correlation with price), not a leading indicator. Divergences are
  noisy, rare, and historically have not reliably predicted tops on this tape.
